newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - LucasVarity plans div growth, buyback.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - LucasVarity plans div growth, buyback.

text.p: Anglo-American engineering giant LucasVarity Plc moved to clear up confusion over its dividend policy on Tuesday, pledging both dividend growth and share buybacks, starting with a three percent share repurchase in 1997.

Victor Rice, chief executive of the auto components to aerospace giant, said this was not a one-off move but a "continuing programme" to satisfy investors on both sides of the Atlantic with a blend of buybacks and dividend growth.
The news came in the group's first set of pro forma results since the merger last September between Britain's Lucas Industries and Varity Corporation of the United States.

LucasVarity, one of the world's top 10 car parts suppliers, said year profits to January 31, 1997 were 282 million pounds ($457.1 million), as expected, with an annual dividend of 2.25 pence per share.
But this would be supplemented with a three percent share buyback, which could be repeated next year, Rice said.
"It's a rolling programme going forward."
The dividend for the year to January 31, 1998 would be 4.5 pence per share, the group said.

LucasVarity's shareprice had been under severe pressure in recent months amid market uncertainty about how it would reward investors. Following the merger, 60 percent of the combined company's shareholders are in Britain and 40 percent in the United States.
Different approaches to rewarding shareholders had led to uncertainty about how the company would alter its dividend policy to satisfy both camps.

In the past British investors from the former Lucas Industries had been used to dividend growth and their last year payout was seven pence per share. U.S. investors from the Varity side of the marriage, however, were used to rewards from buybacks.
Rice said the group had decided on a compromise.
"We expect to see the dividend increase each year in line with profits and continuing share buybacks," he said in an interview.
"It is the most tax efficient mix. We are confident that our cashflow will be able to justify it."
Some analysts remained sceptical, however, about the ability to deliver rising dividends when trading remained tough, particularly in Europe.
"They (LucasVarity) alluded to difficult trading conditions suggesting that operating profits and dividends are not going to storm ahead," said one analyst.
LucasVarity's share price rose to a session high of 208 pence a share, up 7 1/2 pence on the day, on the buyback news but by 1030 GMT had slipped back to 199 1/2p.
Rice said that with markets remaining tough, most of 1997's growth would come from cost savings.
"We see modest growth in our four businesses. But the stronger and better line of growth will be a consequence of the merger," said the chief.
Those savings include 120 million sterling per year by the end of the second year of operations, 140 million pounds of working capital savings and at least 65 million sterling in tax savings.
Total sales for the year were 4.6 billion sterling, up four percent, with operating profits up to 336 million pounds, a rise of five percent.
In a product breakdown, braking systems achieved sales of 1.5 billion sterling, with profits of 121 million pounds versus 116 million previously.

Other automotive businesses saw sales of 1.8 billion pounds, with profits rising to 169 million sterling from 163 million. Diesel engine sales were 655 million pounds, with profits at 59 million sterling versus 55 million.
Aerospace sales were 510 million pounds, with profits up to 49 million sterling from 45 million. ($ = 0.616 British Pounds)
